p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

The "millionaire tax" is back on the California ballot: Proposition 3 would make the 2012 tax rates permanent
Proposition 3 would keep California's top income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% after 2030 instead of letting them drop to 9.3%. The brackets, what it means at $500,000 or $5 million, where the $5 billion to $15 billion goes, and who is paying for the campaign.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 15, 2026

California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The stakes are large and lopsided. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates Prop 3 keeps $5 billion to $15 billion a year in the state budget, collected from the top 2% of taxpayers, who already pay about half of all state income taxes. Supporters frame a yes vote as no tax increase at all; opponents frame it as the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." Both descriptions refer to the same rates. This explainer sets out what the text changes, what the rates mean in dollars, where the money goes (the 89% school figure and the LAO's 40% figure are both right, and measure different things), and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 3 deletes the 2030 end date from the Prop 30 tax rates
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends one section of the Constitution, Article XIII, section 36, which is where Prop 30 put the rates in 2012. The edits are deletions of dates:
In the two paragraphs that set the higher rates, the words "and before January 1, 2031" are struck, so the rates apply "for any taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2012" with no end.
The line in each paragraph that says it "shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031" is struck.
In the rules for the Education Protection Account, the fund that receives the money, end years such as "2030" and "2030–31" become "thereafter."
The rates themselves are unchanged. In the Constitution they are written in 2012 dollars: 10.3% on single-filer income over $250,000, 11.3% over $300,000 and 12.3% over $500,000, with parallel brackets for heads of household, all "recomputed" each year for inflation under the state's normal indexing. The Franchise Tax Board's 2025 rate schedules (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) put those thresholds at $371,479, $445,771 and $742,953 for single filers; $742,958, $891,542 and $1,485,906 for joint filers; and $505,208, $606,251 and $1,010,417 for heads of household. Prop 3 does not touch the separate 1% tax on taxable income above $1 million that voters added for mental health services, now called the Behavioral Health Services Tax. Together the two make California's top marginal rate 13.3% today. If Prop 3 fails, the top rate in 2031 would be 10.3%.
The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure "that affects the tax rates for personal income" is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3.
California income tax rates for top earners are holding at 10.3% to 12.3% under Proposition 3 rather than falling to 9.3% after 2030, with the yearly difference shown at incomes from $400,000 to $5 million in 2026. California income tax rates in dollars: $285 at $400,000, $134,398 at $5 million
The higher rates apply only to the slices of income above each threshold, so their effect starts small and grows quickly. Using the 2025 brackets, we calculated what the Prop 30 rates add to a year's state income tax compared with taxing the same income at 9.3% above the 9.3% threshold. A single filer with $400,000 of taxable income pays $285 more. At $500,000 the difference is $1,828; at $1 million, $14,398; at $5 million, $134,398. Joint filers' brackets are twice as wide: a couple with $500,000 pays nothing extra and a couple with $1 million pays $3,655 more, rising to $28,796 at $2 million and $118,796 at $5 million. These are illustrations at 2025 brackets; by 2031 the thresholds will be higher after inflation indexing.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”
CTA is far from alone in choosing Yes on 3 (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQu1D6GLGe_Yqu1kHb_AGUtbd&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhHMTHFZTUZlUHflSSg6z_2CXI42u6UpgvyIXvgUGaQdt3raGu_PPbhoCid0QAvD_BwE) and No on 40 (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVZHnSZ3kD_EdGrqvCLqPITgu&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhN0sUpdT8Pt04p0vK6yHMXKobIYGrXAwVzXAt3Dm7_oGx_Ifu5UY8BoCZ7QQAvD_BwE). Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone had given $102 million as of late October to stop the billionaire tax, per a data analysis by Capital & Main (https://capitalandmain.com/who-are-the-billionaires-behind-the-304-million-effort-to-defeat-californias-wealth-tax); CTA has given nothing, according to Goldberg.

Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.

The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). It nullifies state taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that exempt revenues from spending limits. Does that "affect the tax rates for personal income"? Arguably — Prop 40's revenue is exempted from spending limits, and Prop 40 is imposed via... hmm, Prop 40 is a tax on net worth collected from individual/fiduciary taxpayers. It could be administered under the Personal Income Tax Law. 
- Prop 42: "Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes" — also would nullify taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that conflict.
- Prop 40: one-time 5% tax on billionaires.

If Prop 3 (polling 54-58% yes) gets more yes votes than Prop 40 (46%), Prop 41, and Prop 42, then under Prop 3's clause, those measures would be "null and void" — assuming a court finds they "affect the tax rates for personal income."

Hmm. That's a big deal but legally uncertain. The Saez/Zucman explainer for Prop 40 says: "The drafters do not expect that this Section would apply to Proposition 3, because that Proposition does not tax net worth..." — but that's about Prop 40's clause applying to Prop 3. It doesn't address Prop 3's clause applying to Prop 40.

Also note: Prop 3's clause says if Prop 3 gets MORE affirmative votes, Prop 3's provisions prevail in their entirety AND the other measure is null and void. So a YES vote on Prop 3 could, in principle, wipe out Prop 40, 41 and 42. But would a court agree that Prop 40 "affects the tax rates for personal income"? Prop 40 is a tax on net worth, not on income rates. However, Prop 40 is administered as... Let me check. Actually the Billionaire Tax Act imposes a tax "on individual and fiduciary taxpayers with more than $1 billion in covered assets" — it would be collected under the Personal Income Tax Law or a new law. Hmm.

Also relevant: Prop 41 and 42 do affect "tax rates for personal income" in a sense — they prohibit new state taxes. Actually Prop 42 prohibits new state taxes on personal property. Prop 41 prohibits new state taxes whose revenues are excluded from the spending limit. Neither directly changes personal income tax rates.

This is legally murky. But it's an argument that Prop 3's clause is a land grab — a poorly drafted, overbroad conflict provision that could create litigation chaos and potentially nullify other voter-approved measures. That's a genuine defect in drafting.

Hmm, but note: the californiatoday.com source says: "The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure 'that affects the tax rates for personal income' is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails 'in their entirety' and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3."

So the LAO did NOT flag Prop 3 as interacting with Props 40/41/42. That reduces the practical concern. But it's still a drafting oddity.

Let me check the californiatoday.com page more, and also look for any analysis of this interaction.

2. **The CTA's "15% budget cut / 1 in 6 educators laid off" claim is not supported by the LAO.** The LAO says ~40% of the revenue goes to schools/colleges — i.e., $2-6B of the $5-15B. Prop 98 is $128.1B in 2026-27. So $4B loss ≈ 3% of Prop 98, not 15%. And enrollment is declining ~710,000 over 10 years, so per-pupil funding would barely change. The CTA's "15%" figure appears to come from "in flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state's overall K-12 education budget" — that's the whole personal income tax, not just the Prop 30 surcharge. So the claim conflates the entire income tax with the surcharge. That's a significant overstatement/misleading claim in the pro argument.

Actually let me be careful: CalMatters said "In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state's overall K-12 education budget." Hmm, that seems low for the income tax — actually personal income tax is a huge share of the General Fund. Whatever. The CTA claim "our public schools face a devastating 15% budget cut" is not consistent with the LAO estimate of ~40% of $5-15B = $2-6B against a $128B Prop 98 budget = 1.5%–4.7%. So the 15% claim is inflated by roughly 3-10x. That's a material misrepresentation in the argument in favor.

3. **The "strict accountability" claim**: The text does contain real provisions — EPA funds can't be used for state administrative costs, local boards have sole authority, can't be used for administrator salaries/benefits, annual online accounting, annual independent audit, AG/DA investigation and civil/criminal penalties for misuse. BUT — crucially — these are all carried over from Prop 30/55 (2012/2016). They're not new. The pro argument presents them as new "strict accountability," when in fact they've been in place since 2012 and haven't prevented the pension-absorption problem. Also, the "no administrative costs" restriction applies at the local district level but the money is general purpose funding that counts toward Prop 98, which the state then offsets.

Also important: the LAO says the audit is already required by existing law (subdivision (e)(7)). So Prop 3 adds essentially nothing new on accountability. It literally just deletes the sunset date. Hoover: "The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets."

So the pro argument's emphasis on "new accountability" is somewhat misleading — it's existing law restated.

4. **Fiscal context**: The state faces structural operating deficits of ~$10-18.5B/yr through 2029-30, and the LAO's November 2025 Fiscal Outlook projected deficits growing to ~$35B annually starting 2027-28. Wait, but then the May Revision said deficits cut in half to ~$10B/yr. And there's a "current revenue boom" tied to an overheated stock market which LAO warns is temporary. So the state's finances are precarious and revenue-dependent on capital gains.

That cuts both ways:
- FOR: The state can't afford to lose $5-15B/yr in 2031 given structural deficits.
- AGAINST: Locking in the most volatile revenue as a permanent base for ongoing spending is exactly what the LAO warns against. And there's Prop 2 on the same ballot to increase the rainy day fund.

5. **Timing/leverage argument (the strongest "No" argument)**: The tax doesn't expire until after 2030 — four years away. There are two more election cycles (2028, 2030) to extend it. A "no" vote now doesn't cut a single dollar of school funding; it simply preserves the option to extend later, possibly with better terms (e.g., pension reform, accountability, sunset, or a broader tax reform). George Skelton (LA Times): "there's no rush. The rates don't expire for five years. No." Also the San Diego U-T editorial board: No. OC Register: No. EdSource commentary: No.

But wait — there's a counter to that: the CTA put it on the 2026 ballot because it's a high-turnout year (midterm with a governor's race). Actually, midterms have lower turnout than presidential years. Hmm, 2026 is a midterm. 2028 and 2030 are presidential/midterm respectively. Actually, the CTA might have chosen 2026 because it's now the "last chance" to lock it in permanently with a favorable climate, or because they didn't want to compete with other tax measures. Also — critically — in 2026 the billionaire-tax fight (Prop 40/41/42) is consuming all the anti-tax money; billionaires are spending $300M+ on Props 41/42 and against 40, and are NOT fighting Prop 3. In fact LA Times notes "No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40." Opposition raised only $5,500 vs. $40M+ for Yes. So 2026 is the cheapest year for the CTA to pass it. In 2028/2030, with Prop 40 settled, the billionaires might turn their firepower against an income tax extension.

Hmm — that's a strategic argument for "vote yes now" (from the CTA's perspective) but from a voter's perspective, it means the measure is passing largely because opposition is unfunded, not because it's been rigorously vetted.

6. **Empirical evidence on behavioral response**: Genuinely contested.
- Rauh & Shyu (AEJ: Policy 2024, peer-reviewed): Prop 30 responses eroded 45.2% of windfall revenue in year 1, 60.9% in 2 years, mostly intensive margin (elasticity of taxable income 2.5-3.2 w.r.t. net-of-tax rate — that's very high; typical literature estimates for top earners are 0.2-0.5 overall, though much higher for capital gains realization).
- Young, Varner, Lurie, Slemrod: find little migration response in CA to top tax rate changes; millionaire migration elasticity ~0.1 nationally (Young et al.), small.
- Kleven/Landais/Saez: small migration elasticities.
So the migration effect is likely small; the income-reporting effect is more contested. An ETI of 2.5-3.2 is far above mainstream estimates (~0.25-0.5 for broad income, higher for capital gains ~1.0). Rauh's estimate is an outlier but published in a top field journal (AEJ: Policy). 

However, note: even if 45-60% of the revenue is eroded, the tax still raises substantial revenue — the LAO says $5-15B/yr and actual collections have been ~$10B/yr recently, with $120B cumulative since 2012. So the "money loser" claim (that marginal revenue is negative) is a strong claim not well supported: if the revenue were negative, the state wouldn't have collected $10B/yr. Rauh/Kearney argue that since 2018 the state loses more from departures/base erosion than it collects — that seems implausible given observed collections. The Budget Center says ~$10B/yr in recent years. So "money loser" is almost certainly overstated; the more defensible claim is "the revenue is smaller than the static estimate."

Important nuance: the LAO's $5-15B estimate is a *static* estimate of what the surcharge collects. Actual FTB data shows it does collect billions. So even with big behavioral responses, it's a significant revenue source.

7. **Where the money goes**: Only ~40% actually increases school funding; ~60% backfills other General Fund programs. Rauh/Kearney: K-12 district pension contributions nearly tripled 2015-2023 to ~$13B; pension share of school employee spending went from ~7% to >13%; pension increases consumed 44% of the increase in school budgets. So a large share of new school money went to pensions rather than classrooms. This undercuts the "every dollar to classrooms" claim, though the pro side would say pensions are compensation for educators.

8. **Progressivity/equity**: Top 2% pay ~half of state income taxes. Top 1% real incomes grew 2.5x over four decades while bottom 80% declined. Median CA family income ~$100k; the surcharge starts at $371k single/$743k joint. This is a genuinely progressive measure that doesn't touch middle-class taxes.

9. **Cost of living / competitiveness**: CA has the highest top marginal rate (13.3%, 14.6% with SDI). Net domestic out-migration; CA lost >100,000 net tax filers to other states 2022-2023. High cost of living. Making rates permanent further entrenches this.

Now — how to decide?

Let me think about this as a careful voter weighing the evidence.

Arguments that should carry the most weight:

(a) **It's not a tax increase on anyone today.** True. But compared to current law (which sunsets in 2031), it IS a $5-15B/yr tax increase from 2031 forward. The honest framing matters: this is a decision about the 2031-and-beyond tax structure.

(b) **Does California need the revenue?** Overwhelmingly yes. The state has persistent structural operating deficits ($10-18.5B/yr per DOF, LAO projecting larger). Losing $5-15B/yr in 2031 would force either deep cuts (schools, Medi-Cal, universities, courts, fire) or a new tax increase fought under worse conditions. Prop 3 essentially pre-commits to the revenue.

(c) **Who bears it?** Top ~2% of filers, thresholds $371k single / $743k joint (inflation-adjusted), rising to 12.3% and 13.3% above $1M. Median CA household income ~$100k. The vast majority of Californians pay nothing extra. This is about as progressive and as narrowly targeted as a tax gets.

(d) **Does it deliver for schools?** Partially — ~40% net new to schools/CCCs, ~60% frees General Fund for Medi-Cal, UC/CSU, reserves. That's still $2-6B/yr to schools and the rest supports health care and other services. Notably: the federal government cut Medicaid significantly (HR 1), and California estimates ~$30B/yr in losses — so the freed-up General Fund dollars have a real use.

(e) **Is the "15% cut / 1 in 6 educators laid off" claim credible?** No — it's inflated. LAO implies ~3-5% of Prop 98. And enrollment is falling ~7% over a decade, so per-pupil funding would be roughly flat. This is a demerit for the Yes campaign's honesty.

(f) **Is the "new strict accountability" claim credible?** No — the audit, anti-administration, and transparency provisions are all carried over verbatim from Prop 30/55 (2012/2016). Prop 3 adds no new accountability. Another demerit for the Yes campaign.

(g) **Permanence in the constitution.** This is the strongest principled objection. Tax rates embedded in the state constitution can only be changed by another statewide vote; the Legislature can't adjust them in response to economic change. Skelton (LA Times) and the SD U-T board both cite this. It also locks in reliance on the most volatile revenue stream (capital gains) as a permanent base for ongoing spending — which is exactly the structural weakness the LAO repeatedly warns about.

(h) **Behavioral response.** Contested. Rauh/Shyu (peer-reviewed) found large erosion of Prop 30's revenue; Young/Varner/Slemrod and Kleven/Landais/Saez found small effects. The truth is probably in between: the tax raises real revenue but less than static estimates suggest, and there's some efficiency cost. The "net money loser" claim is not credible given ~$10B/yr in actual collections.

(i) **Timing.** The rates don't expire until after the 2030 tax year. A "no" vote costs nothing today; there are 2028 and 2030 elections to extend. This significantly lowers the stakes of a "no."

(j) **Interaction with the rest of the ballot.** Prop 40 (one-time billionaire wealth tax) is likely to be nullified by Props 41/42 anyway. Prop 41/42 would ban future wealth taxes and retroactive taxes. Prop 2 expands the rainy day fund. Prop 3's own overbroad conflicting-measures clause ("any other measure that affects the tax rates for personal income" → null and void if Prop 3 gets more yes votes) is sloppy drafting that could generate litigation; the LAO didn't flag an interaction, so practical risk seems low.

(k) **Funding asymmetry.** Yes on 3 raised $40M+ (CTA $33.3M, NEA $10M, later reports $58M); No on 3 raised $5,500. This is a measure passing largely unopposed — which means voters have had little exposure to the counterarguments and the measure hasn't been stress-tested. Also, the billionaire camp deliberately declined to fight Prop 3 (preferring it to Prop 40). That's a reason for skepticism about the campaign's messaging but not necessarily about the policy.

Now, weighing:

The case for YES:
- Protects $5-15B/yr of revenue that the state's structurally-deficit budget genuinely depends on.
- Falls only on top 2%, thresholds well above median income; no middle-class impact.
- Voting no doesn't force a reform; it just creates a 2031 revenue cliff that would likely be resolved either by deep cuts or by another, more desperate tax fight.
- Broad, credible support: SF Chronicle, McClatchy/Bay Area News Group (Sac Bee, Mercury News, East Bay Times, SLO Tribune), teachers, nurses, PTA, firefighters, Children Now; even billionaires who oppose Prop 40 support it. 58% of likely voters.
- The alternative — letting it expire — is effectively a $5-15B/yr tax cut concentrated on the top 1%, at a time when the state faces federal Medicaid cuts and structural deficits.
- California's schools remain underfunded relative to need (1:22 student-teacher ratio vs. 1:15 national).

The case for NO:
- Permanence: constitutionalizes tax rates, removing legislative flexibility and future voter review.
- Misleading campaign: inflated 15%/50,000-teacher-layoff claim; "new accountability" that is actually 2012-era boilerplate; "89% to schools" when LAO says ~40% net.
- Volatility: locks in the most volatile revenue as the base for ongoing spending — the LAO's repeated warning.
- Behavioral/economic evidence (Rauh/Shyu) that the top brackets collect materially less than the static estimate, plus CA's highest-in-nation rates and out-migration.
- Money largely absorbed by pensions and administrative cost growth; LAUSD insolvency despite record funding; enrollment declining 9 straight years.
- No urgency: expires after 2030; two more ballot cycles to extend, and a "no" now preserves leverage to demand real reform (pension, accountability) in exchange.
- Structural imbalance: state spending doubled while population flat.

Hmm. This is genuinely close. Let me think about which consideration should be decisive.

Key question: What is the actual consequence of each vote?

- YES: The rates continue forever. No change for 99% of Californians. The state keeps $5-15B/yr from 2031 onward, of which ~40% net goes to schools and ~60% frees General Fund for health care/other. Risk: entrenches volatile revenue, removes future flexibility, no further voter check.

- NO: Nothing happens until 2031. The CTA/legislature can and almost certainly will put an extension on the 2028 or 2030 ballot. Realistically the probability that California actually lets these rates lapse in 2031 with no extension attempt is low — no legislature facing an $18B structural deficit will allow a $10B revenue loss without a fight. So the practical downside of NO is small and reversible; the practical effect of NO is to deny permanence and keep the sunset as leverage.

That's a strong argument: NO is the low-risk, high-option-value vote. But there's a counter: if the extension fight happens in 2030, it will be against the backdrop of an actual fiscal cliff, likely with demands for even higher taxes or a broader tax, and with the same money. Also, "kicking the can" has its own cost — uncertainty for school districts' multi-year planning (the CTA's stated rationale). And the CTA has already spent $58M; making them do it again in 2028/2030 has real political costs.

But is uncertainty a big deal? Districts plan 2-3 years out; the sunset is 4+ years away. And Prop 55's own extension in 2016 happened only 4 years before expiry.

Now, what about the merits of the underlying policy? Is a permanent 10.3-13.3% marginal rate on income above $371k good tax policy for California?

Arguments it's reasonable:
- Highly progressive; thresholds far above median.
- Revenue funds universal public goods (schools, Medi-Cal).
- CA already has this rate and the economy has performed well (though the LAO warns about the stock market boom being temporary).
- The top 1%'s share of income has grown enormously; asking them to maintain current rates is not onerous.
- Even with behavioral responses, net revenue is positive and large (~$10B/yr).

Arguments it's bad policy:
- 13.3% top rate (14.6% with SDI) is the nation's highest; combined with the federal rate (and post-TCJA SALT cap) it pushes total marginal rates near 50%+.
- Concentration risk: top 1% pays ~40-50% of PIT; revenue swings 55% up / 35% down.
- Making it permanent constitutionalizes this and forecloses the more sensible reform (broadening the base, lowering rates, stabilizing revenue) that the LAO and others have long recommended.
- Evidence (Rauh/Shyu, AEJ:Policy 2024) that CA's high earners respond substantially.
- CA is losing population and businesses; the tax structure is part of the cost-of-living/competitiveness problem.

Honestly, on the pure economics, the evidence is mixed and the strongest empirical work specific to this exact tax (Rauh & Shyu, AEJ: Policy) suggests substantial revenue erosion — but not a net loss. And on the fiscal side, the state clearly needs the revenue.

Let me weigh what I think is decisive: the combination of (1) the state's genuine structural deficit and reliance on this revenue, (2) the narrowly targeted progressivity (top 2%, thresholds $371k+), (3) the fact that a NO vote is effectively a $5-15B/yr tax cut for the top 1% scheduled for 2031 with no accompanying spending reform or replacement revenue on offer, and (4) the absence of any credible reform package attached to the "no" side — the "no" campaign is essentially Howard Jarvis/CalTax saying "fix spending first," which is not a plan.

Against that: the misleading campaign claims and the permanence/constitutionalization concern.

Hmm. The misleading claims are a real problem. But they're about the *campaign*, not the *policy*. The policy is: keep existing rates on the top 2% instead of cutting them.

Let me think about the "permanence" objection more carefully, because it's the strongest substantive one. Is it actually bad to put these rates in the constitution permanently?

California already constitutionalizes a great deal of fiscal policy: Prop 98 (school funding formula), Prop 13 (property tax), Prop 2/Prop 58 (reserves), Prop 63 (mental health surtax — permanent since 2004), Prop 111 (state spending limit). The 1% millionaire surtax from Prop 63 (2004) has been permanent for 22 years and nobody proposes repealing it. So permanence per se isn't anomalous in California.

But the "no future voter check" argument is weakened by the fact that voters can always amend the constitution again. Permanence ≠ irrevocability; it just means the default is continuation. And the default under current law (sunset) means the default is a massive cut unless voters act. Given that the state has extended it twice already (2016 with 63% yes), and given polling at 54-58%, the realistic counterfactual is that the sunset is a recurring, expensive, uncertainty-generating ritual — not a genuine accountability mechanism. That's a decent argument for YES: the sunset has proven to be a fake constraint that just generates budget uncertainty every ~14 years.

Counter-counter: But the sunset is what gives voters leverage to demand accountability. If it's permanent, there's no leverage. Though — has the sunset produced any accountability? Prop 55 in 2016 did add the Medi-Cal allocation and audit language. So yes, the 2016 extension did extract something. Hmm, that's a fair point: the sunset mechanism produced the Medi-Cal allocation and audit provisions in Prop 55.

But Prop 3 arguably also adds... nothing new. Let me double check: does Prop 3 add anything relative to Prop 55? Let me compare. Prop 55 (2016) extended through 2030 and added: the Medi-Cal allocation (50% of excess up to $2B), audit requirements, the prohibition on administrative costs, annual online accounting, AG/DA enforcement. Prop 3's text as shown includes all of those — carried over. So Prop 3 = Prop 55 minus the sunset. Confirmed by Hoover: "The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date."

So voters are being offered the exact same deal with no new accountability, and the Yes campaign is advertising existing 2016 provisions as if they were new ("Prop. 3 includes Constitutional protections and tough accountability... Every dollar is independently audited every year"). That's a real honesty problem. A well-informed voter could reasonably conclude: "You're asking me to give up my only leverage point, forever, and you're adding nothing in return — while telling me the accountability is new when it's a decade old, and telling me schools will be cut 15% when your own nonpartisan analyst says ~40% of $5-15B goes to schools."

Hmm, this is pushing me toward NO.

But let me also weigh: what does the "no" side offer? "Fix spending first." Concretely: nothing. And the "no" side is funded with $5,500 — i.e., it's not a serious campaign. The people actually arguing no are Howard Jarvis, CalTax, and Susan Shelley. Their substantive points (permanence, volatility, pensions, enrollment decline) are real, but their proposed remedy is inaction.

Let me consider the actual budget math once more. In 2031, if these rates lapse:
- General Fund loses $5-15B (call it $10B).
- Prop 98 guarantee falls by ~40% of that (~$4B) since it's formula-driven off GF revenue.
- Non-Prop-98 programs lose ~$6B.
- The state would face that on top of an existing structural deficit.
So the "no" outcome is a real fiscal hole. Would the Legislature fill it? They'd need a 2/3 vote for a new tax, or a ballot measure. Or cuts. Given California politics (supermajority Democrats), they'd likely put a new/extended tax on the 2028 or 2030 ballot. In fact, the CTA explicitly says: "If it fails, the union will have two more chances."

So the realistic counterfactual of a NO vote is: another extension measure in 2028 or 2030, probably temporary again. The policy outcome is likely similar; the difference is delay, uncertainty, and campaign spending.

Given that, the question becomes: do you want to lock it in permanently now, or keep re-voting?

Let me now think about which answer better serves the voter's interest and the public interest.

I think the decisive consideration is this: **Prop 3 asks voters to permanently surrender their only point of leverage over a $5–15 billion/year revenue stream, in exchange for nothing new — while the campaign for it relies on materially inflated claims (a "15% school cut" and "1 in 6 educators laid off" that the LAO's own numbers contradict; and "new" accountability provisions that are actually unchanged 2016 boilerplate). And it does so at a moment when there is no fiscal urgency, because the rates don't expire for another four years and two more statewide elections intervene.**

Hmm, but is that enough to outweigh the fact that the underlying tax is progressive, needed, and that a "no" is functionally a scheduled tax cut for the top 1%?

Let me look for a few more things to firm this up:
1. Does the LAO or anyone estimate what schools actually lose? I have: LAO says ~40% to schools/CCCs. Prop 98 = $128.1B. So $2-6B = 1.6%-4.7%.
2. What's the CTA's basis for 15%? Let me check if there's a fact-check. The Pasadena Star-News piece effectively debunks it. Also let me check EdSource's own reporting.
3. Any additional "no" endorsements? Let me check who wrote the EdSource "no" commentary.
4. Let me check the LA Times Skelton piece and the SD U-T editorial for their reasoning.
5. Also: is there any evidence about whether Prop 30 revenue actually improved school outcomes? 

Let me also double check the claim that "opponents raised $5,500" — that's remarkable. And check the latest contribution totals.

Actually, one more crucial thing I should check: whether the "no" side's concern about stacking is real. In 2026, Californians are also voting on Prop 40 (one-time 5% billionaire tax). If both Prop 3 and Prop 40 pass, high-earners face a permanent 13.3% income tax plus a one-time wealth tax. But Prop 40 is likely dead due to 41/42.

Let me also consider: Newsom endorsed Prop 42 (which bans wealth taxes). Interesting — so the Democratic governor is on the anti-wealth-tax side but presumably not opposing Prop 3.

Let me do a couple more searches to firm up: the EdSource no-op-ed author, the LA Times Prop 3 explainer ("partly true"), and the measure contribution totals.

Actually, I think I have enough to reason. But let me get two more things: (1) the LA Times piece "Prop. 3 is being touted by unions as a school funding bill. That's partly true" — this is a good neutral assessment; (2) confirm campaign finance asymmetry; (3) check the EdSource no-op-ed.

Let me fetch those.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”
CTA is far from alone in choosing Yes on 3 (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQu1D6GLGe_Yqu1kHb_AGUtbd&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhHMTHFZTUZlUHflSSg6z_2CXI42u6UpgvyIXvgUGaQdt3raGu_PPbhoCid0QAvD_BwE) and No on 40 (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVZHnSZ3kD_EdGrqvCLqPITgu&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhN0sUpdT8Pt04p0vK6yHMXKobIYGrXAwVzXAt3Dm7_oGx_Ifu5UY8BoCZ7QQAvD_BwE). Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone had given $102 million as of late October to stop the billionaire tax, per a data analysis by Capital & Main (https://capitalandmain.com/who-are-the-billionaires-behind-the-304-million-effort-to-defeat-californias-wealth-tax); CTA has given nothing, according to Goldberg.

Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.

The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
