(a) In 2012, California voters passed a tax increase on
high-income earners—the top 2%—to fund critical
state services and stave off extreme cuts to public
education brought on by the fiscal challenges of the
Great Recession. These tax rates were extended by the
voters in 2016, with 63% voting yes. Since its initial
passage, this tax measure has raised more than $104
billion for schools and other essential services. It is a
foundational part of the state budget and the state
Rainy Day Fund.
3 (b) This high-earner income tax has allowed the state
to make important investments in the education and
health of our children and has helped California’s
public school system become more competitive among
the 50 states. In 2012, California ranked in the bottom
10 among the states in school spending. Today, with
these revenues, California has made real progress in
school spending. Our state now provides free school
meals; free transitional kindergarten to all four-year-
olds; free before-and-after school care for younger
elementary students; and community services in many
school districts.
(c) Unless the tax is extended by the voters, it will
expire in 2030. That would result in an immediate

PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. 5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

If Prop 3 fails, and the state still wants the revenue, the Legislature can't extend it without a 2/3 vote + it'd be a new tax... Actually the Legislature could place a measure on the ballot to extend it. So it's not a one-shot deal.

Now, let me think about the merits carefully.

Key considerations for a thoughtful voter:

FOR (Yes):
1. It's not a tax increase relative to today; it maintains the status quo. Voting no would create a $5-15B/year revenue cliff in 2031.
2. California faces persistent structural deficits ($10-18B operating deficits through 2029-30, LAO projected $35B structural deficits from 2027-28). Losing $5-15B/year in 2031 would force deep cuts.
3. The revenue is heavily concentrated on the top 2%, who pay ~half of income taxes; it's progressive.
4. School funding: California per-pupil spending has improved; K-12 enrollment declining but class sizes still among the largest; TK, universal meals, etc., all rely on ongoing revenue.
5. Federal cuts to Medi-Cal (~$30B/year estimate) mean health care needs backfill.
6. Broad support: 58% PPIC likely voters; supported by teachers, nurses, PTA, firefighters; even some billionaires who oppose Prop 40 support Prop 3 (per LA Times).

AGAINST (No):
1. "Temporary" taxes made permanent — voters were promised sunset. Removes future accountability/leverage. It's a constitutional amendment, so only voters can change it.
2. Revenue volatility: it locks in the most volatile revenue source as the base for ongoing spending. LAO: swings $5-15B.
3. Behavioral response evidence (Rauh/Shyu): Prop 30 erased 45% of expected revenue gain in year 1, 61% within 2 years; Rauh/Kearney argue since 2018 (post-TCJA SALT cap) the top brackets may be net revenue losers. If true, making them permanent is fiscally counterproductive. Though this is contested — other studies (e.g., Stanford/CBO, and the LAO's own analyses) find modest migration effects. Kleven/Landais/Saez find small elasticities for top earners. There's genuine academic disagreement.
4. The money doesn't actually reach classrooms as promised: only ~40% net increases school funding; pension costs have absorbed much of school funding growth (district pension contributions nearly tripled 2015-2023).
5. Declining enrollment: K-12 enrollment down 500,000+ since mid-2010s; per-pupil spending already among highest-adjusted; the "50,000 teacher layoffs" claim is a projection, not a certainty.
6. California's high taxes/high cost of life driving out-migration overall (net domestic out-migration), hurting the tax base broadly.
7. Spending problem: state spending doubled while population flat; $100B surplus → $30B deficit in three years (rhetorically charged but directionally there is a structural imbalance).
8. Stacking with Prop 40 (one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax) and other proposed taxes (health insurance tax, software tax) — cumulative burden on a narrow base.

Now: how should I weigh these? The user asks "What should I vote?" and wants a yes/no answer. I should make a decision and justify it.

Let me gather a bit more evidence, especially:
- The academic literature dispute on millionaire migration (Saez/Kleven vs. Rauh). The Hoover claim of "net revenue loser" is a strong claim; mainstream public finance (Kleven, Landais, Saez 2013; Slemrod; Young et al.) generally finds small elasticities. But there is CA-specific evidence. Let me look at the LAO's own view and the Tax Foundation.
- Editorial endorsements — a good proxy for informed centrist opinion.

So CTA's 15% claim seems way off — actually maybe they mean 15% of the general purpose funding increase or something. Worth checking. Actually hold on: if the EPA revenue ($10B) counts toward Prop 98 and 89% goes to K-12 ($8.9B), then losing it would reduce Prop 98 by... hmm. Actually the Prop 98 guarantee is formula-based on General Fund revenues and attendance; if the surcharge revenue disappears, total GF revenues fall, so the Prop 98 guarantee itself falls by roughly 40% of the revenue loss (~$4B), and the rest is absorbed by non-Prop-98 programs. So schools lose ~$4B (3.5% of Prop 98) not 15%. Unless the state chose to backfill. So the CTA claim of a 15% cut / 50,000 teacher layoffs appears inflated. PUBLISHED: October 29, 2026 at 1:49 PM PDT

The strongest argument against Proposition 3, the statewide ballot measure that would permanently extend temporary income tax increases on high earners first passed in 2012, is the fiscal train wreck of the Los Angeles Unified School District.
The California Teachers Association has spent (https://edsource.org/updates/heres-how-much-california-teachers-association-has-spent-on-barrera-campaign-prop-3) more than $58 million to place this tax increase on the ballot and persuade voters to approve it. CTA president David Goldberg signed the argument in favor of Prop. 3, calling it necessary to prevent “teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and bigger class sizes.”
The first thing to know about education in California is that it’s funded every year with roughly 40% of the general fund under Proposition 98 (1988). So as revenue grows, funding for kindergarten through community college also grows, without a tax increase.
Then there’s the enrollment decline to consider. The CTA is using tried-and-true talking points from another time in history. The number of students in California’s public schools has declined (https://dof.ca.gov/forecasting/demographics/public-k-12-graded-enrollment/) for nine consecutive years. The 10-year projection from the state’s Department of Finance predicts a decline of another 710,500 in total enrollment. In 2021-22, the “Census Day” snapshot of enrollment was 5,892,240, but enrollment is expected to fall to 5.021 million in 2035-36.
The largest decline will be in Los Angeles County, projected to finish the next ten years with 240,800 fewer students.
The argument for Prop. 3 warns that if the measure fails on November 3, $15 billion a year will be stripped from the schools. That’s the high end of the estimated revenue reduction. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says it could be $5 billion.
These are big numbers, but they amount to only a fraction of the education budget. Final numbers for the 2024-25 budget show (https://www.lao.ca.gov/Education/EdBudget/Details/1130) $124.9 billion went to K-14 education under the Prop. 98 guarantee. The current budget for 2026-27 estimates Prop. 98 funding for education at $128.1 billion.
If funding is going up and enrollment is going down, where’s the money going?
This is where LAUSD can very educational, for taxpayers, that is. The nation’s second-largest school district earned the designation of “not a going concern” after it disregarded warnings about the cost of proposed labor union contracts for the district’s employees, agreeing to the new contracts without having the money to pay for them.
On July 2, acting under state law established for exactly this purpose, the Los Angeles County Superintendent of Schools determined that LAUSD would run out of operating cash to pay its bills during the 2027-28 fiscal year. The district would also have reserves below the state-required minimum and continuing structural deficits.
The county superintendent flagged declining enrollment and attendance, spending reductions that were never implemented even though they were part of a “Fiscal Stabilization Plan,” and the fiscal impact of the recently approved collective bargaining agreements.
The “lack of going concern” designation triggered a mandatory Fiscal Health Risk Analysis by FCMAT, the Fiscal Crisis & Management Assistance Team. FCMAT was created by the California Legislature to provide help to local educational agencies that are plunging toward fiscal insolvency. FCMAT provides school district officials with professional learning resources, software, checklists, manuals and other tools.

Hmm, but is that enough to outweigh the fact that the underlying tax is progressive, needed, and that a "no" is functionally a scheduled tax cut for the top 1%?

Let me look for a few more things to firm this up:
1. Does the LAO or anyone estimate what schools actually lose? I have: LAO says ~40% to schools/CCCs. Prop 98 = $128.1B. So $2-6B = 1.6%-4.7%.
2. What's the CTA's basis for 15%? Let me check if there's a fact-check. The Pasadena Star-News piece effectively debunks it. Also let me check EdSource's own reporting.
3. Any additional "no" endorsements? Let me check who wrote the EdSource "no" commentary.
4. Let me check the LA Times Skelton piece and the SD U-T editorial for their reasoning.
5. Also: is there any evidence about whether Prop 30 revenue actually improved school outcomes? 

Let me also double check the claim that "opponents raised $5,500" — that's remarkable. And check the latest contribution totals.

Actually, one more crucial thing I should check: whether the "no" side's concern about stacking is real. In 2026, Californians are also voting on Prop 40 (one-time 5% billionaire tax). If both Prop 3 and Prop 40 pass, high-earners face a permanent 13.3% income tax plus a one-time wealth tax. But Prop 40 is likely dead due to 41/42.

Let me also consider: Newsom endorsed Prop 42 (which bans wealth taxes). Interesting — so the Democratic governor is on the anti-wealth-tax side but presumably not opposing Prop 3.

Let me do a couple more searches to firm up: the EdSource no-op-ed author, the LA Times Prop 3 explainer ("partly true"), and the measure contribution totals.

Actually, I think I have enough to reason. But let me get two more things: (1) the LA Times piece "Prop. 3 is being touted by unions as a school funding bill. That's partly true" — this is a good neutral assessment; (2) confirm campaign finance asymmetry; (3) check the EdSource no-op-ed.

Let me fetch those.

1. **Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause (SEC. 5)** is unusually aggressive: "In the event that this measure and another measure **that affects the tax rates for personal income** shall appear on the same statewide ballot, the provisions of the other measure or measures shall be deemed to be in conflict with this measure. In the event that this measure receives a greater number of affirmative votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict with it, the provisions of this measure shall prevail **in their entirety**, and the other measure or measures shall be **null and void**."

Note the asymmetry: Prop 40's conflict clause is narrower (applies only to measures taxing billionaire net worth). Prop 41 and 42's clauses also are targeted. But Prop 3's clause is broad — "another measure that affects the tax rates for personal income."

Do Props 41 and 42 "affect the tax rates for personal income"?

Arguably — Prop 40's revenue is exempted from spending limits, and Prop 40 is imposed via... hmm, Prop 40 is a tax on net worth collected from individual/fiduciary taxpayers. It could be administered under the Personal Income Tax Law.

Hmm. That's a big deal but legally uncertain. The Saez/Zucman explainer for Prop 40 says: "The drafters do not expect that this Section would apply to Proposition 3, because that Proposition does not tax net worth..." — but that's about Prop 40's clause applying to Prop 3. Also note: Prop 3's clause says if Prop 3 gets MORE affirmative votes, Prop 3's provisions prevail in their entirety AND the other measure is null and void. So a YES vote on Prop 3 could, in principle, wipe out Prop 40, 41 and 42. But would a court agree that Prop 40 "affects the tax rates for personal income"? Prop 40 is a tax on net worth, not on income rates. However, Prop 40 is administered as... Let me check. Actually the Billionaire Tax Act imposes a tax "on individual and fiduciary taxpayers with more than $1 billion in covered assets" — it would be collected under the Personal Income Tax Law or a new law. Hmm, but note: the californiatoday.com source says: "The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure 'that affects the tax rates for personal income' is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails 'in their entirety' and the other measure is void. So the LAO did NOT flag Prop 3 as interacting with Props 40/41/42. That reduces the practical concern. But it's still a drafting oddity.

Let me check the californiatoday.com page more, and also look for any analysis of this interaction.

The CTA's "15%" figure appears to come from "in flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state's overall K-12 education budget" — that's the whole personal income tax, not just the Prop 30 surcharge. So the claim conflates the entire income tax with the surcharge. That's a significant overstatement/misleading claim in the pro argument.

Actually let me be careful: CalMatters said "In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state's overall K-12 education budget." Hmm, that seems low for the income tax — actually personal income tax is a huge share of the General Fund. Whatever. The CTA claim "our public schools face a devastating 15% budget cut" is not consistent with the LAO estimate of ~40% of $5-15B = $2-6B against a $128B Prop 98 budget = 1.5%–4.7%. So the 15% claim is inflated by roughly 3-10x. That's a material misrepresentation in the argument in favor.

BUT — crucially — these are all carried over from Prop 30/55 (2012/2016). They're not new. The pro argument presents them as new "strict accountability," when in fact they've been in place since 2012 and haven't prevented the pension-absorption problem. Also, the "no administrative costs" restriction applies at the local district level but the money is general purpose funding that counts toward Prop 98, which the state then offsets.

Also important: the LAO says the audit is already required by existing law (subdivision (e)(7)). So Prop 3 adds essentially nothing new on accountability. It literally just deletes the sunset date. Hoover: "The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets."

So the pro argument's emphasis on "new accountability" is somewhat misleading — it's existing law restated.

Wait, but then the May Revision said deficits cut in half to ~$10B/yr. And there's a "current revenue boom" tied to an overheated stock market which LAO warns is temporary. So the state's finances are precarious and revenue-dependent on capital gains.

That cuts both ways:
- FOR: The state can't afford to lose $5-15B/yr in 2031 given structural deficits.
- AGAINST: Locking in the most volatile revenue as a permanent base for ongoing spending is exactly what the LAO warns against. And there's Prop 2 on the same ballot to increase the rainy day fund.

A "no" vote now doesn't cut a single dollar of school funding; it simply preserves the option to extend later, possibly with better terms (e.g., pension reform, accountability, sunset, or a broader tax reform). George Skelton (LA Times): "there's no rush. The rates don't expire for five years. No." Also the San Diego U-T editorial board: No. OC Register: No. EdSource commentary: No.

But wait — there's a counter to that: the CTA put it on the 2026 ballot because it's a high-turnout year (midterm with a governor's race). Actually, midterms have lower turnout than presidential years. Hmm, 2026 is a midterm. 2028 and 2030 are presidential/midterm respectively. Actually, the CTA might have chosen 2026 because it's now the "last chance" to lock it in permanently with a favorable climate, or because they didn't want to compete with other tax measures. Also — critically — in 2026 the billionaire-tax fight (Prop 40/41/42) is consuming all the anti-tax money; billionaires are spending $300M+ on Props 41/42 and against 40, and are NOT fighting Prop 3. In fact LA Times notes "No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40." Opposition raised only $5,500 vs. $40M+ for Yes. So 2026 is the cheapest year for the CTA to pass it. In 2028/2030, with Prop 40 settled, the billionaires might turn their firepower against an income tax extension.

Hmm — that's a strategic argument for "vote yes now" (from the CTA's perspective) but from a voter's perspective, it means the measure is passing largely because opposition is unfunded, not because it's been rigorously vetted.

Let me think about this as a careful voter weighing the evidence.

Arguments that should carry the most weight:

(a) **It's not a tax increase on anyone today.** True. But compared to current law (which sunsets in 2031), it IS a $5-15B/yr tax increase from 2031 forward. The honest framing matters: this is a decision about the 2031-and-beyond tax structure.

(b) **Does California need the revenue?** Overwhelmingly yes. The state has persistent structural operating deficits ($10-18.5B/yr per DOF, LAO projecting larger). (c) **Who bears it?** Top ~2% of filers, thresholds $371k single / $743k joint (inflation-adjusted), rising to 12.3% and 13.3% above $1M. Median CA household income ~$100k. The vast majority of Californians pay nothing extra. This is about as progressive and as narrowly targeted as a tax gets.

(d) **Does it deliver for schools?** Partially — ~40% net new to schools/CCCs, ~60% frees General Fund for Medi-Cal, UC/CSU, reserves. That's still $2-6B/yr to schools and the rest supports health care and other services. Notably: the federal government cut Medicaid significantly (HR 1), and California estimates ~$30B/yr in losses — so the freed-up General Fund dollars have a real use.

(f) **Is the "new strict accountability" claim credible?** No — the audit, anti-administration, and transparency provisions are all carried over verbatim from Prop 30/55 (2012/2016). Prop 3 adds no new accountability. Another demerit for the Yes campaign.

(g) **Permanence in the constitution.** This is the strongest principled objection. Tax rates embedded in the state constitution can only be changed by another statewide vote; the Legislature can't adjust them in response to economic change. Skelton (LA Times) and the SD U-T board both cite this. It also locks in reliance on the most volatile revenue stream (capital gains) as a permanent base for ongoing spending — which is exactly the structural weakness the LAO repeatedly warns about.

(h) **Behavioral response.** Contested. Rauh/Shyu (peer-reviewed) found large erosion of Prop 30's revenue; Young/Varner/Slemrod and Kleven/Landais/Saez found small effects. This is a measure passing largely unopposed — which means voters have had little exposure to the counterarguments and the measure hasn't been stress-tested. Also, the billionaire camp deliberately declined to fight Prop 3 (preferring it to Prop 40). That's a reason for skepticism about the campaign's messaging but not necessarily about the policy.

Now, weighing:

The case for YES:
- Protects $5-15B/yr of revenue that the state's structurally-deficit budget genuinely depends on.
- Falls only on top 2%, thresholds well above median income; no middle-class impact.
- Voting no doesn't force a reform; it just creates a 2031 revenue cliff that would likely be resolved either by deep cuts or by another, more desperate tax fight.
- Broad, credible support: SF Chronicle, McClatchy/Bay Area News Group (Sac Bee, Mercury News, East Bay Times, SLO Tribune), teachers, nurses, PTA, firefighters, Children Now; even billionaires who oppose Prop 40 support it. 58% of likely voters.
- The alternative — letting it expire — is effectively a $5-15B/yr tax cut concentrated on the top 1%, at a time when the state faces federal Medicaid cuts and structural deficits.
- California's schools remain underfunded relative to need (1:22 student-teacher ratio vs. 1:15 national).

The case for NO:
- Permanence: constitutionalizes tax rates, removing legislative flexibility and future voter review.
- Misleading campaign: inflated 15%/50,000-teacher-layoff claim; "new accountability" that is actually 2012-era boilerplate; "89% to schools" when LAO says ~40% net.
- Volatility: locks in the most volatile revenue as the base for ongoing spending — the LAO's repeated warning.
- Behavioral/economic evidence (Rauh/Shyu) that the top brackets collect materially less than the static estimate, plus CA's highest-in-nation rates and out-migration.
- Money largely absorbed by pensions and administrative cost growth; LAUSD insolvency despite record funding; enrollment declining 9 straight years.
- No urgency: expires after 2030; two more ballot cycles to extend, and a "no" now preserves leverage to demand real reform (pension, accountability) in exchange.
- Structural imbalance: state spending doubled while population flat.

Hmm. This is genuinely close. Let me think about which consideration should be decisive.

Key question: What is the actual consequence of each vote?

- YES: The rates continue forever. No change for 99% of Californians. The state keeps $5-15B/yr from 2031 onward, of which ~40% net goes to schools and ~60% frees General Fund for health care/other. Risk: entrenches volatile revenue, removes future flexibility, no further voter check.

- NO: Nothing happens until 2031. The CTA/legislature can and almost certainly will put an extension on the 2028 or 2030 ballot. Realistically the probability that California actually lets these rates lapse in 2031 with no extension attempt is low — no legislature facing an $18B structural deficit will allow a $10B revenue loss without a fight. So the practical downside of NO is small and reversible; the practical effect of NO is to deny permanence and keep the sunset as leverage.

That's a strong argument: NO is the low-risk, high-option-value vote. But there's a counter: if the extension fight happens in 2030, it will be against the backdrop of an actual fiscal cliff, likely with demands for even higher taxes or a broader tax, and with the same money. Also, "kicking the can" has its own cost — uncertainty for school districts' multi-year planning (the CTA's stated rationale). And the CTA has already spent $58M; making them do it again in 2028/2030 has real political costs.

But is uncertainty a big deal? Districts plan 2-3 years out; the sunset is 4+ years away. And Prop 55's own extension in 2016 happened only 4 years before expiry.

Now, what about the merits of the underlying policy? Is a permanent 10.3-13.3% marginal rate on income above $371k good tax policy for California?

Arguments it's reasonable:
- Highly progressive; thresholds far above median.
- Revenue funds universal public goods (schools, Medi-Cal).
- CA already has this rate and the economy has performed well (though the LAO warns about the stock market boom being temporary).
- The top 1%'s share of income has grown enormously; asking them to maintain current rates is not onerous.
- Even with behavioral responses, net revenue is positive and large (~$10B/yr).

Arguments it's bad policy:
- 13.3% top rate (14.6% with SDI) is the nation's highest; combined with the federal rate (and post-TCJA SALT cap) it pushes total marginal rates near 50%+.
- Concentration risk: top 1% pays ~40-50% of PIT; revenue swings 55% up / 35% down.
- Making it permanent constitutionalizes this and forecloses the more sensible reform (broadening the base, lowering rates, stabilizing revenue) that the LAO and others have long recommended.
- Evidence (Rauh/Shyu, AEJ:Policy 2024) that CA's high earners respond substantially.
- CA is losing population and businesses; the tax structure is part of the cost-of-living/competitiveness problem.

Honestly, on the pure economics, the evidence is mixed and the strongest empirical work specific to this exact tax (Rauh & Shyu, AEJ: Policy) suggests substantial revenue erosion — but not a net loss. And on the fiscal side, the state clearly needs the revenue.

Let me weigh what I think is decisive: the combination of (1) the state's genuine structural deficit and reliance on this revenue, (2) the narrowly targeted progressivity (top 2%, thresholds $371k+), (3) the fact that a NO vote is effectively a $5-15B/yr tax cut for the top 1% scheduled for 2031 with no accompanying spending reform or replacement revenue on offer, and (4) the absence of any credible reform package attached to the "no" side — the "no" campaign is essentially Howard Jarvis/CalTax saying "fix spending first," which is not a plan.

Against that: the misleading campaign claims and the permanence/constitutionalization concern.

Hmm. The misleading claims are a real problem. But they're about the *campaign*, not the *policy*. The policy is: keep existing rates on the top 2% instead of cutting them.

Let me think about the "permanence" objection more carefully, because it's the strongest substantive one. Is it actually bad to put these rates in the constitution permanently?

California already constitutionalizes a great deal of fiscal policy: Prop 98 (school funding formula), Prop 13 (property tax), Prop 2/Prop 58 (reserves), Prop 63 (mental health surtax — permanent since 2004), Prop 111 (state spending limit). The 1% millionaire surtax from Prop 63 (2004) has been permanent for 22 years and nobody proposes repealing it. So permanence per se isn't anomalous in California.

But the "no future voter check" argument is weakened by the fact that voters can always amend the constitution again. Permanence ≠ irrevocability; it just means the default is continuation. And the default under current law (sunset) means the default is a massive cut unless voters act. Given that the state has extended it twice already (2016 with 63% yes), and given polling at 54-58%, the realistic counterfactual is that the sunset is a recurring, expensive, uncertainty-generating ritual — not a genuine accountability mechanism. That's a decent argument for YES: the sunset has proven to be a fake constraint that just generates budget uncertainty every ~14 years.

Counter-counter: But the sunset is what gives voters leverage to demand accountability. If it's permanent, there's no leverage. Though — has the sunset produced any accountability? Hmm, that's a fair point: the sunset mechanism produced the Medi-Cal allocation and audit provisions in Prop 55.

Prop 55 (2016) extended through 2030 and added: the Medi-Cal allocation (50% of excess up to $2B), audit requirements, the prohibition on administrative costs, annual online accounting, AG/DA enforcement. Prop 3's text as shown includes all of those — carried over. So Prop 3 = Prop 55 minus the sunset. Confirmed by Hoover: "The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date."

So voters are being offered the exact same deal with no new accountability, and the Yes campaign is advertising existing 2016 provisions as if they were new ("Prop. 3 includes Constitutional protections and tough accountability... Every dollar is independently audited every year"). That's a real honesty problem. A well-informed voter could reasonably conclude: "You're asking me to give up my only leverage point, forever, and you're adding nothing in return — while telling me the accountability is new when it's a decade old, and telling me schools will be cut 15% when your own nonpartisan analyst says ~40% of $5-15B goes to schools."

Hmm, this is pushing me toward NO.

But let me also weigh: what does the "no" side offer? "Fix spending first." Concretely: nothing. And the "no" side is funded with $5,500 — i.e., it's not a serious campaign. The people actually arguing no are Howard Jarvis, CalTax, and Susan Shelley. Let me consider the actual budget math once more. In 2031, if these rates lapse:

- Prop 98 guarantee falls by ~40% of that (~$4B) since it's formula-driven off GF revenue.
- Non-Prop-98 programs lose ~$6B.
- The state would face that on top of an existing structural deficit.
So the "no" outcome is a real fiscal hole. Would the Legislature fill it? They'd need a 2/3 vote for a new tax, or a ballot measure. Or cuts. Given California politics (supermajority Democrats), they'd likely put a new/extended tax on the 2028 or 2030 ballot. In fact, the CTA explicitly says: "If it fails, the union will have two more chances."

So the realistic counterfactual of a NO vote is: another extension measure in 2028 or 2030, probably temporary again. The policy outcome is likely similar; the difference is delay, uncertainty, and campaign spending.

Given that, the question becomes: do you want to lock it in permanently now, or keep re-voting?

Let me now think about which answer better serves the voter's interest and the public interest.

I think the decisive consideration is this: **Prop 3 asks voters to permanently surrender their only point of leverage over a $5–15 billion/year revenue stream, in exchange for nothing new — while the campaign for it relies on materially inflated claims (a "15% school cut" and "1 in 6 educators laid off" that the LAO's own numbers contradict; and "new" accountability provisions that are actually unchanged 2016 boilerplate). And it does so at a moment when there is no fiscal urgency, because the rates don't expire for another four years and two more statewide elections intervene.**

Hmm, but is that enough to outweigh the fact that the underlying tax is progressive, needed, and that a "no" is functionally a scheduled tax cut for the top 1%?

Let me look for a few more things to firm this up:
1. Does the LAO or anyone estimate what schools actually lose? I have: LAO says ~40% to schools/CCCs. Prop 98 = $128.1B. So $2-6B = 1.6%-4.7%.
2. What's the CTA's basis for 15%? Let me check if there's a fact-check. The Pasadena Star-News piece effectively debunks it. Also let me check EdSource's own reporting.

5. Also: is there any evidence about whether Prop 30 revenue actually improved school outcomes? 

Let me also double check the claim that "opponents raised $5,500" — that's remarkable. And check the latest contribution totals.

If both Prop 3 and Prop 40 pass, high-earners face a permanent 13.3% income tax plus a one-time wealth tax. But Prop 40 is likely dead due to 41/42.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The well-funded campaign for Proposition 3 describes it as a direly needed tool for funding public schools.
“Prop. 3 maintains critical funding for local schools, preventing larger class sizes and teacher layoffs,” says a video ad on YouTube. “Every dollar goes to local schools, not politicians in Sacramento.”
In reality, the ballot initiative is another tax measure on high-income Californians, this one helping to pay for all state services supported by general fund dollars, including healthcare, courts and schools. In other words, schools are the sales pitch to voters for a tax measure that affects considerably more than schools.
Advertisement
The measure has huge support from California’s largest teachers union, and it is separate from Proposition 40, the billionaire tax measure. No one is staunchly fighting Proposition 3 — including the group of billionaires who would rather see it pass than 40.
Proposition 3 would make permanent higher tax rates on about the highest-earning 2% of the state’s tax filers, rates that would otherwise expire at the end of 2030. If these tax rates were allowed to expire, the state’s general fund would absorb a massive annual hit of an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in today’s dollars.
Of the money raised by this tax, about 40% goes to funds that pay for transitional kindergarten through community college. About 60% goes to other areas — healthcare, in-home supportive services, higher education, the prison system, the court system and more. That explains why a broad coalition of unions supports the Yes on Proposition 3 campaign, even if the overriding pitch is about schools.
Advertisement
The biggest spender in support of Proposition 3 is the California Teachers Assn. — which poured about $60 million into promoting it through Monday and has harnessed its vast membership for on-the-ground canvassing. The teachers union has embraced Proposition 3 as a more strategic alternative to Proposition 40, which a mid-September poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax)found has divided likely voters.
Support has been strong for Proposition 3, although public polling also has been more limited.
Propositions 40 and 3 each would benefit schools. But the teachers union is uncomfortable with how Proposition 40 is structured. Union leaders also worry that two tax-the-rich measures could confuse voters and turn them against both — especially given the massive campaign billionaires are waging against Proposition 40.
“When you have hundreds of millions of dollars being spent against the idea of raising revenue, I think that does impact the general voter zeitgeist,” said CTA President David Goldberg. “There’s always a fear that voters can get overwhelmed and confused, and voters can just say, ‘I’ve had enough,’ and just vote against everything.”
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1. It is projected to raise tens of billions of dollars — mostly for healthcare. Prop. 40, in some respects, is a direct, albeit temporary, response (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) to phased-in health- and social-service cuts in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed in July 2025.
For educators, said Goldberg, Proposition 3 is the better bet than Proposition 40 because a greater percentage of 3 goes to education and its benefit would be ongoing.
Advertisement
“The funding for Prop. 3 has become a huge and an essential part of our education funding in California,” Goldberg said. “Making it permanent is vitally important. We are a labor-intensive kind of work, so potentially up to one in six educators could be looking at layoff notices at the end of this decade. And the impact would be felt even earlier as districts would start to prepare and hold back reserves.”
Other donors of $1 million or more (https://project-voter-guide-2026.interactives.calmatters.org/general/en/campaign-finance/prop/3) to Yes on 3 include, as compiled by a CalMatters database: National Education Assn.; California School Employees Assn.; CFT — a separate California teachers union; and the California arm of the Service Employees International Union as well as SEIU Local 2015, which represents in-home care providers and nursing home staff.
It adds up to more than $81 million for and about $5,500 against.
Odd bedfellows
In a case of odd bedfellows, Building a Better California, the billionaire-funded group bankrolling the fight against the billionaire tax, has endorsed Proposition 3.
Proposition 3 keeps rates billionaires already pay on income — and appears likely to pass — while Proposition 40 would, in total, subtract billions from their net worth. Their explanation (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/faq) is that “we believe in strong, accountable investments that will strengthen our state, protect our schools, address the housing crisis, and improve other essential public services.”
CTA is far from alone in choosing Yes on 3 (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQu1D6GLGe_Yqu1kHb_AGUtbd&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhHMTHFZTUZlUHflSSg6z_2CXI42u6UpgvyIXvgUGaQdt3raGu_PPbhoCid0QAvD_BwE) and No on 40 (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVZHnSZ3kD_EdGrqvCLqPITgu&gclid=CjwKCAjwl4HXBhAjEiwAHlpWhN0sUpdT8Pt04p0vK6yHMXKobIYGrXAwVzXAt3Dm7_oGx_Ifu5UY8BoCZ7QQAvD_BwE). Others in that camp include California Medical Assn., California Professional Firefighters, United Domestic Workers, Gov. Gavin Newsom and gubernatorial front-runner Xavier Becerra.
The main No on 40 committee is fronted by doctors, teachers, firefighters and unions, but nearly 100% of its money has come from Building a Better California, the group overwhelmingly funded by tech billionaires.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone had given $102 million as of late October to stop the billionaire tax, per a data analysis by Capital & Main (https://capitalandmain.com/who-are-the-billionaires-behind-the-304-million-effort-to-defeat-californias-wealth-tax); CTA has given nothing, according to Goldberg.

Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
